note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: How many children and young people are out of school worldwide?
questions.whyCorrect: 272 million — and the number has actually gone UP by 3% since 2015. Over half of them live in sub-Saharan Africa.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Work out how many schools it would take to hold 272 million children.

questions.prompt: In low-income countries, what share of school-aged children are out of school?
questions.whyCorrect: 36% — against just 3% in high-income countries. Where you're born is the single biggest predictor of whether you'll go to school.
whyWrong: That's the high-income figure.
Too high — though the real gap is enormous.
questions.action: Compare 36% and 3%. That's a twelvefold difference.

questions.prompt: How many adults still cannot read and write?
questions.whyCorrect: 754 million adults — and 63% of them are women. Illiteracy is not evenly distributed between the sexes.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Imagine trying to use a bus timetable or medicine label without reading.

questions.prompt: Of the world's 754 million illiterate adults, what share are women?
questions.whyCorrect: 63% — nearly two-thirds. When families can only afford to educate some children, girls are more often the ones who miss out.
whyWrong: It isn't an even split.
Far too low — women are the majority.
questions.action: Ask why a family might educate a son before a daughter.

questions.prompt: What share of primary school children worldwide can read at a minimum level?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 58%. More than four in ten children finish primary years without basic reading ability — being in school isn't the same as learning.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic, though the real figure is alarming.
Far too optimistic.
questions.action: Notice the difference between attending school and learning.

questions.prompt: What share of primary children reach minimum maths proficiency?
questions.whyCorrect: Just 44% — even lower than reading at 58%. The majority of the world's children are not learning basic maths.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
Too pessimistic, though the real figure is very low.
questions.action: Ask what 'minimum proficiency' should mean at age 10.

questions.prompt: In richer countries, learning scores between 2018 and 2022 did what?
questions.whyCorrect: They fell — maths down 15 percentage points and reading down 10 across 81 upper-middle and high-income countries. School closures hit learning hard.
whyWrong: Scores dropped substantially in this period.
There was a marked decline.
questions.action: Ask an older student what remote learning was actually like.

questions.prompt: What share of primary schools worldwide lack electricity, drinking water or a toilet?
questions.whyCorrect: More than one school in five lacks at least one of these basics. It's hard to learn without light, water or somewhere to go to the toilet.
whyWrong: Ten times too optimistic.
Too high globally, though it's true of least developed countries.
questions.action: List everything your school has that a school without electricity doesn't.

questions.prompt: In the least developed countries, what share of schools have no electricity?
questions.whyCorrect: More than half. Over two-thirds also lack digital tools, and over a third lack sanitation.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
Ten times too optimistic.
questions.action: Ask what lessons become impossible without power.

questions.prompt: What share of schools worldwide have computers or internet?
questions.whyCorrect: Fewer than 50% have computers, internet, or facilities adapted for disabled students. The digital divide starts in the classroom.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic globally.
Too pessimistic — nearly half do have them.
questions.action: Count the computers in your school.

questions.prompt: Globally, who performs better at school — girls or boys?
questions.whyCorrect: Girls outperform boys at all levels by 2–3 percentage points — even though girls are more likely to be kept out of school entirely.
whyWrong: There's a consistent measurable gap.
It runs the other way.
questions.action: Ask why girls do better once they're actually in the classroom.

questions.prompt: How many countries have equal numbers of men and women in university?
questions.whyCorrect: Just 5% of countries achieve gender parity in university enrolment. In most places the numbers are lopsided one way or the other.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
Very few countries achieve parity.
questions.action: Look up the gender split at a university near you.

questions.prompt: What share of children complete primary school?
questions.whyCorrect: 88%, up from 85% in 2015. Good — but it still means roughly one child in eight never finishes primary school.
whyWrong: Too optimistic — millions don't complete.
That's closer to the upper secondary figure.
questions.action: Work out what 12% of the world's children is in real numbers.

questions.prompt: What share of young people complete upper secondary school — the equivalent of finishing high school?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 60%, up from 53% in 2015. Four in ten young people worldwide never finish secondary education.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — most do complete.
Far too optimistic globally.
questions.action: Ask what jobs need a completed secondary education.

questions.prompt: How many children aged 3 to 5 attend pre-primary education?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 40%, and participation has been stuck around 50% since 2015. Early years shape everything that follows, yet most children miss them.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
Too pessimistic — four in ten do attend.
questions.action: Ask why the years before age 5 matter so much.

questions.prompt: In sub-Saharan Africa, what share of young children attend pre-primary school?
questions.whyCorrect: 27% — well below the global 40%. Northern Africa and Western Asia is similar at 30%.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — over a quarter attend.
Far too optimistic for the region.
questions.action: Compare 27% with the global figure of 40%.

questions.prompt: What share of children aged 2 to 5 are developing normally for their age?
questions.whyCorrect: Two-thirds are on track — meaning about a third of the world's young children are already falling behind before school even starts.
whyWrong: Far too pessimistic.
Too optimistic — a third are not on track.
questions.action: Ask what helps a toddler's brain develop.

questions.prompt: Youth literacy worldwide is now about:
questions.whyCorrect: 93%, up from 91% a decade ago. Young people are far more literate than older generations — adult literacy is 88%.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — youth literacy is high.
Too optimistic — millions of young people still can't read.
questions.action: Compare youth literacy (93%) with adult (88%). Why the gap?

questions.prompt: How many adults aged 25 to 54 took part in any education or training last year?
questions.whyCorrect: Just 3%. For people over 55 it's 1%. 'Lifelong learning' is a goal that barely exists in practice for most adults.
whyWrong: Ten times too optimistic.
Far too optimistic.
questions.action: Ask an adult when they last took a class.

questions.prompt: Among young people aged 15 to 24, what share are in education or training?
questions.whyCorrect: Over 50%, ranging from 45% in sub-Saharan Africa to 64% in Europe and North America.
whyWrong: Far too pessimistic.
Too optimistic — nearly half are not.
questions.action: Ask what the other half are doing instead.

questions.prompt: The number of out-of-school children since 2015 has:
questions.whyCorrect: It rose 3%. Education is one of the goals where the world has moved backwards rather than forwards.
whyWrong: There was a measurable rise.
It increased rather than decreased.
questions.action: Ask what pushed more children out of school after 2015.

questions.prompt: Where do over half of all out-of-school children live?
questions.whyCorrect: More than half of the 272 million out-of-school children are in sub-Saharan Africa — the region with the fastest-growing young population.
whyWrong: Europe has near-universal school attendance.
South America has high enrolment rates.
questions.action: Look up how many children will be school-age in Africa by 2050.

questions.prompt: Which is harder to achieve — getting children into school, or getting them to learn?
questions.whyCorrect: 88% complete primary school but only 58% can read at a minimum level. Attendance has improved far faster than actual learning.
whyWrong: Enrolment has improved much faster than learning outcomes.
The learning gap is substantially wider.
questions.action: Ask what makes a lesson actually work.

questions.prompt: How many countries fail to achieve gender parity at upper secondary completion?
questions.whyCorrect: 83% of countries. Gender gaps widen as education goes on — 40% lack parity at primary, over 50% at lower secondary, 83% at upper secondary.
whyWrong: Very few countries achieve parity at this level.
Far too optimistic.
questions.action: Notice how the gap widens with each stage of education.

questions.prompt: Lower secondary completion is now about:
questions.whyCorrect: 78%, up from 74% in 2015. Slow progress — roughly one young person in five doesn't finish.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic.
Too optimistic — over a fifth don't complete.
questions.action: Compare 88% primary, 78% lower secondary, 60% upper secondary.

questions.prompt: School electricity access has improved since 2015 by roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: More than 10 percentage points in eight years — real progress, though over 20% of schools still lack basics.
whyWrong: Access improved rather than declined.
The improvement was much larger.
questions.action: Ask what solar power could do for a rural school.

questions.prompt: Among young people tested on digital skills, what were they weakest at?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 57% were proficient in online safety — the lowest of all digital skills tested, below communication (83%) and information literacy (76%).
whyWrong: This scored 76%, well above safety.
This was the strongest skill at 83%.
questions.action: Test yourself: could you spot a scam message?

questions.prompt: How many children lack basic drinking water at school?
questions.whyCorrect: 447 million children have no basic drinking water at school, and 427 million lack sanitation.
whyWrong: A hundred times too low.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Ask how long you'd last at school without water.

questions.prompt: What share of schools provide basic hygiene facilities like handwashing?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 67% — leaving 646 million children at school without anywhere to wash their hands properly.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — two-thirds do have them.
Far too optimistic.
questions.action: Count the handwashing points in your school.

questions.prompt: Adult literacy worldwide is now:
questions.whyCorrect: 88%, up from 85%. That still leaves 754 million adults unable to read this sentence.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — most adults are literate.
Too optimistic — hundreds of millions cannot read.
questions.action: Ask what daily tasks need reading.

questions.prompt: Upper secondary completion rose from 53% in 2015 to 60%. Is that fast enough?
questions.whyCorrect: Progress decelerated to just 0.8 percentage points a year. At that pace universal secondary education is many decades away.
whyWrong: The target will be missed by a wide margin.
It slowed rather than sped up.
questions.action: Work out how long 40 more percentage points takes at 0.8 a year.

questions.prompt: In sub-Saharan Africa, what share of young people are in education or training?
questions.whyCorrect: 45%, against 64% in Europe and North America — a 19-point gap in access to learning after childhood.
whyWrong: That's closer to the European figure.
Too pessimistic — nearly half participate.
questions.action: Ask what happens to young people not in school or training.

questions.prompt: What share of countries lack gender parity at primary completion?
questions.whyCorrect: 40% of countries. Even at the most basic level of education, boys and girls complete at different rates in four countries out of ten.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
Too high — most countries do reach parity at primary level.
questions.action: Compare 40% at primary with 83% at upper secondary.

questions.prompt: In the least developed countries, what share of schools lack digital tools?
questions.whyCorrect: Over 67% have no computers or internet at all — meaning most students there will finish school having never used one.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
Too optimistic — the real figure is over two-thirds.
questions.action: Ask what jobs require digital skills you learned at school.

questions.prompt: How many adults aged 55 to 64 take part in education or training?
questions.whyCorrect: Just 1%. Learning effectively stops for almost everyone once they leave formal education.
whyWrong: Vastly too optimistic.
Far too optimistic.
questions.action: Ask an older relative what they'd like to learn.

questions.prompt: Which basic school facility is most commonly missing worldwide?
questions.whyCorrect: Fewer than half of schools have computers, internet, or facilities adapted for disabled students — the most commonly missing of the measured basics.
whyWrong: Not among the tracked global indicators.
Not among the tracked global indicators.
questions.action: Check whether your school is accessible to a wheelchair user.

questions.prompt: Maths proficiency compared with reading proficiency at primary level is:
questions.whyCorrect: Maths lags reading by 14 percentage points. Fewer than half the world's primary children can do basic maths.
whyWrong: There's a substantial gap between them.
It's the other way round.
questions.action: Ask why maths might be harder to teach than reading.

questions.prompt: One in six people aged 15 to 64 took part in education last year. What does that suggest?
options: Education is evenly spread across life
questions.whyCorrect: Over half of 15–24s participate, but only 3% of 25–54s and 1% of over-55s. Learning is concentrated almost entirely in youth.
whyWrong: Only 3% of working-age adults participated.
It's heavily concentrated in the youngest group.
questions.action: Ask what would make adult learning easier where you live.

questions.prompt: Primary completion rose from 85% to 88% between 2015 and 2024. How would you describe that?
questions.whyCorrect: Three percentage points in nine years. Real, but far too slow to reach every child by 2030.
whyWrong: Three points in nine years is modest.
Completion rose rather than fell.
questions.action: Ask what it would take to reach the last 12%.

questions.prompt: Which region has the lowest pre-primary participation?
questions.whyCorrect: Sub-Saharan Africa at 27%, just below Northern Africa and Western Asia at 30%, against a global average of 40%.
whyWrong: Europe has among the highest participation.
North America has high participation.
questions.action: Ask what a child gains from two years of pre-school.

questions.prompt: Learning scores fell in richer countries after 2018. What's the most likely cause?
questions.whyCorrect: Maths fell 15 points and reading 10 across 81 countries in the 2018–2022 window — the period covering worldwide school closures.
whyWrong: The tests were designed to be comparable over time.
Enrolment didn't collapse in these countries.
questions.action: Ask how much school time was lost where you live.

questions.prompt: Of the 272 million out-of-school children, the number has changed since 2015 by:
questions.whyCorrect: It rose 3%. Population growth outpaced the expansion of school places, so more children are out of school than a decade ago.
whyWrong: This is the opposite of what happened.
The number rose rather than fell.
questions.action: Ask how population growth affects school planning.

questions.prompt: In least developed countries, what share of schools lack sanitation?
questions.whyCorrect: Over 33% have no sanitation. For girls especially, no toilet at school often means not attending at all during their period.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic.
Too high, though the real figure is serious.
questions.action: Ask why a school toilet matters more for girls.

questions.prompt: How many children lack basic sanitation at school?
questions.whyCorrect: 427 million children have no basic sanitation where they learn — alongside 447 million with no drinking water.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Ask what you'd do at school with no toilet available.

questions.prompt: Which digital skill were young people strongest at?
questions.whyCorrect: Communication and collaboration at 83% — young people are good at connecting, weaker at creating content (60%) and staying safe (57%).
whyWrong: This scored 60%, well below communication.
This was the weakest at 57%.
questions.action: Rate yourself honestly on all five skills.

questions.prompt: What share of schools have basic drinking water?
questions.whyCorrect: 77% — leaving 447 million children at schools with no safe water to drink during the day.
whyWrong: Too optimistic — nearly a quarter of schools lack it.
Too pessimistic — most schools do have water.
questions.action: Find the nearest drinking water in your school.

questions.prompt: Girls are more likely than boys to be out of school, yet once in school they:
questions.whyCorrect: Girls outperform boys by 2–3 percentage points at every level. The barrier is access, not ability.
whyWrong: The data shows girls ahead once enrolled.
There's a consistent gap in girls' favour.
questions.action: Ask what stops a girl attending school in some countries.

questions.prompt: Early childhood education participation since 2015 has:
questions.whyCorrect: It's been stuck near 50% for a decade — no meaningful progress on the stage of education that shapes everything after it.
whyWrong: There has been essentially no growth.
It held steady rather than falling.
questions.action: Ask why early years get less funding than later ones.

questions.prompt: In high-income countries, what share of children are out of school?
questions.whyCorrect: 3% — twelve times lower than the 36% in low-income countries. Even wealthy countries don't reach every child.
whyWrong: That's closer to the low-income figure of 36%.
No country reaches literally every child.
questions.action: Ask who the 3% in rich countries might be.

questions.prompt: What's the clearest sign that being in school isn't enough on its own?
options: 88% finish primary but only 58% can read
questions.whyCorrect: The 30-point gap between completing primary school and being able to read is the sharpest evidence that attendance and learning are different problems.
whyWrong: Important, but the completion-versus-literacy gap is the direct evidence.
This is about access, not about learning inside school.
questions.action: Ask what your school does to check you're actually learning.
